name: Tazarotene
lead: Tazarotene, sold as Tazorac, Arazlo and other brands, is a third-generation acetylenic topical retinoid used for acne vulgaris and plaque psoriasis. Certain formulations are also used to reduce signs of photoaging such as fine facial wrinkles and mottled pigmentation. It is a prodrug converted in the skin to the active tazarotenic acid [1][2]. It was approved for medical use in 1997 and is available as a generic [1].

It is generally regarded as a potent topical retinoid, and irritation is a recurring limiting factor, which has driven newer lotion and foam formulations and combination products [1][3][4]. A 2024 US guideline strongly recommends topical retinoids as a class for acne [5].

Tazarotene is a known teratogen and is contraindicated in pregnancy; the US label requires a negative pregnancy test within two weeks before starting in people who could become pregnant, plus effective contraception [2]. It is prescription-only.
infobox: Topical retinoid (acetylenic, third generation; RAR beta/gamma selective)

paras: Tazarotene gel 0.05 and 0.1 percent was effective in clinical trials in plaque psoriasis, with the effect maintained for at least 12 weeks after stopping in some patients, and combination with a mid- or high-potency corticosteroid was more effective than tazarotene alone [6]. For acne, a 1998 drug review reported that tazarotene 0.1 percent gel significantly reduced lesion counts in mild to moderate acne [6]. Like other retinoids it can be used with benzoyl peroxide or an antibiotic for added efficacy [1].

The cream form is used on photodamaged skin and can reduce histological and clinical signs including fine lines, wrinkles, hyperpigmentation and lentigines, with greater effect when used with daily sunscreen [1]. A BMJ Clinical Evidence systematic review addressed interventions for wrinkles [7], and a Skin Therapy Letter article summarised a multicentre randomized trial of tazarotene 0.1 percent cream for photodamage [8]. A pilot study combined tazarotene with azelaic acid, tacrolimus and zinc oxide in melasma [9].

Tazarotene is available as gels, creams, foams and lotions at concentrations from 0.045 to 0.1 percent. It was first approved in 1997 as 0.05 and 0.1 percent gel, creams followed in 2000, a 0.1 percent aerosol foam in 2012 for hair-bearing or large areas, and a 0.045 percent polymeric-emulsion lotion in 2019. A fixed-dose halobetasol/tazarotene combination is available for psoriasis [1].

Tazarotene is converted by deesterification to tazarotenic acid, which binds all three retinoic acid receptors but is relatively selective for RAR beta and gamma [2]. It affects keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, upregulating filaggrin and downregulating transglutaminase, involucrin and various keratins [1]. It induces the tazarotene-induced genes, including TIG2, whose product was later identified as a ligand for the receptor ChemR23 [10][11].
Tazarotenic acid is more than 99 percent protein bound, and elimination is via feces and urine in equal parts with a half-life of 16 to 18 hours [1].

Irritation (redness, itching, burning, peeling) is the usual effect and tends to increase with concentration; on the US label the most common reactions occurred in 10 to 23 percent of psoriasis patients (pruritus, erythema, burning) and 10 to 30 percent of acne patients [1][2]. Photosensitivity and sunburn risk are warned about [2].

Before 2015 tazarotene was FDA Category X for pregnancy while tretinoin and adapalene were Category C, despite similar plasma retinoid levels; under the revised labeling rule it is contraindicated on the basis of teratogenic effects in rats and rabbits and the absence of pregnancy-outcome data [1]. A literature review has examined tazarotene use in acne in pregnancy [12].

Acne: registered trials include a 1,077-patient study comparing tazarotene 0.1 percent cream with Tazorac and placebo, a 1,110-patient phase 3 study of the 0.1 percent cream, an 893-patient phase 3 study of 0.1 percent foam, a pharmacokinetic and bioavailability study of a new formulation (58 patients), and a 78-patient safety and pharmacokinetic study of the 0.045 percent lotion [13][14][15][16][17]. A phase 4 study compared dapsone plus tazarotene with tazarotene alone in 171 patients [18]. A phase 3 trial reported effects of tazarotene 0.045 percent lotion on quality of life in moderate-to-severe acne [19].

Tolerability: two double-blind 12-day patch studies in 20 healthy adults each found tazarotene 0.045 percent lotion mildly irritating and lower in irritation than adapalene 0.3 percent gel, and in the second study significantly less irritating than trifarotene 0.005 percent cream [3]. A randomized facial tolerability study of topical retinoids was also published in 2004 [20].

Psoriasis: an 855-patient phase 3 study compared tazarotene 0.05 percent cream with Tazorac and placebo, and a pooled phase 3 analysis assessed halobetasol 0.01 percent / tazarotene 0.045 percent lotion on lower extremities [21][22].
Photodamage: a multicenter randomized trial of 0.1 percent cream is summarised in the Skin Therapy Letter [8].

Other conditions: small registered studies examined tazarotene for basal cell skin cancer in basal cell nevus syndrome (36 patients), brittle nails (20) and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (15), and a randomized trial evaluated minocycline and/or topical tazarotene for cetuximab-related acneiform rash in 48 patients [23][24][25]. Laboratory work has explored tazarotene effects on melanoma cell growth [26].

Tazarotene is prescription-only and generic. Wikipedia notes its use alongside other retinoids and in regimens with benzoyl peroxide or antibiotics [1]. No community discussion of tazarotene was found in the forum sources reviewed for this wiki.

timeline.event: Tazarotene approved for medical use as 0.05% and 0.1% gel [1].
